The filing states the strike "disrupted our St. Louis operations and impacting programs including F/A-18, F-15, T-7A Red Hawk, MQ-25 and Weapons" (pp.4, 26). It also notes the stoppage occurred **even though** a tentative agreement had been reached with union leadership and leadership had recommended ratification — i.e., the membership rejected it (p.11).

I reviewed Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K (BA_2024_10K.pdf) body (Parts I–IV, Items 1–15 and the consolidated financial statements/notes), excluding exhibits. Here are the dollar amounts the filing gives for dividends on the 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock.

## The three dividend amounts

**1. $345 million** — Item 1A, "Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity" (p. 19)
> "We also expect to require up to $345 million of cash per year for the payment of dividends on the outstanding shares of our 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock (Mandatory convertible preferred stock), through the mandatory conversion date of October 15, 2027."

This is a forward-looking annual cash-requirement estimate, not an amount actually paid or accrued in 2024.

**2. $58 million** — Consolidated Statements of Operations (p. 56), Note 4 – Earnings Per Share (p. 77), and Note 23 segment reconciliation (p. 63)
> "Less: Mandatory convertible preferred stock dividends accumulated during the period 58"

This is the preferred dividend **accrued during 2024** (the stub period from the October 31, 2024 issuance date through December 31, 2024). It is deducted from net loss attributable to Boeing shareholders of $(11,817) million to arrive at net loss attributable to Boeing common shareholders of $(11,875) million, and is the numerator adjustment in the basic/diluted loss-per-share computation ($18.36 per share). It was a non-cash accrual; no preferred dividends were paid in cash during 2024.

**3. $72 million** — Note 19 – Shareholders' Equity (p. 110) and the Consolidated Statements of Equity (p. 62)
> "In December 2024, dividends of $72 were declared to holders of record as of January 1, 2025, representing $12.50 per share, and were paid in cash on January 15, 2025."

This is the **full quarterly dividend declared** in December 2024 ($12.50 per share on 5,750,000 shares ≈ $71.9 million). It appears in the equity statement as "Cash dividends declared on Mandatory convertible preferred stock (72)" reducing retained earnings. Because the record date was January 1, 2025 and payment was made January 15, 2025, the $72 million is a 2025 cash outflow, not a 2024 one.

## Notes on related figures that are not dividend amounts
- The $5,651 million net cash proceeds (Note 19), the $5,657 million "Mandatory convertible preferred stock issuance, net of issuance costs" line in financing activities (p. 60), and the $5,645 million credited to additional paid-in capital (p. 62) are issuance proceeds, not dividends.
- The $5,750 million aggregate liquidation preference and the $6 million par value on the balance sheet (p. 58) are capital/liquidation amounts, not dividends.
- The $12.50 per share figure is the quarterly per-share dividend rate, not a dollar total of dividends paid.

So, on a dollar-total basis, the filing gives two 2024 amounts — $58 million accrued and $72 million declared (paid in January 2025) — plus the forward-looking $345 million annual cash requirement through the October 15, 2027 mandatory conversion.

- Disclosure thresholds only: the "10% or more" tests for customers/vendors and for country-level net sales and long-lived assets (U.S., China), plus the "majority," "significant" and "substantial" qualitative concentration language in the risk factors.

One thing to note: Apple does **not** disclose any percentage of fiscal 2025 net sales attributable to a specific customer or to Google/search-licensing arrangements, so the only net-sales percentage tied to a channel or counterparty grouping in the filing is the 40%/60% direct-versus-indirect split.

## NVIDIA FY2024 Form 10‑K — Inventory‑related charges and releases to cost of revenue

Source: NVDA_2024_10K.pdf (fiscal year ended January 28, 2024)

### 1. Total provisions charged to cost of revenue (MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin," p. 40)
- **$2.2 billion** — "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $2.2 billion for both fiscal years 2024 and 2023." This is the combined fiscal 2024 charge to cost of revenue for (a) excess/obsolete inventory write-downs and (b) excess inventory purchase obligations.

### 2. The two components of that $2.2 billion (Note 10, Balance Sheet Components)

| Component | Fiscal 2024 amount charged to cost of revenue | Source / what it represents |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory provision (excess/obsolete inventory write-down) | **$774 million** | Note 10 footnote to the Inventories table (p. 68): "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an inventory provision of $774 million and $1.0 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue." Write-down of inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value for excess or obsolete quantities (per the Note 1 "Inventories" policy, p. 58). |
| Inventory purchase obligations in excess of demand projections | **approximately $1.4 billion** | Note 10 footnote to Accrued and Other Current Liabilities (p. 70): "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an expense of approximately $1.4 billion and $1.1 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue for inventory purchase obligations in excess of our current demand projections, supplier charges and for penalties related to cancellations and underutilization." |

(The $774 million + ~$1.4 billion approximates the $2.2 billion total provision disclosed in MD&A.)

### 3. Provision release (MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin," p. 40)
- **$540 million** — "Sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations resulted in a provision release of $540 million and $137 million for fiscal years 2024 and 2023, respectively." This is a credit to cost of revenue, arising either from selling previously written-down/reserved inventory (which had already established a new, non-reversible cost basis per Note 1) or from settling excess inventory purchase obligations at less than the amount provided.

### 4. Net effect
- Fiscal 2024 net charge to cost of revenue = **$2.2 billion of provisions less the $540 million release ≈ $1.66 billion net** (the filing states this as an unfavorable gross margin impact of 2.7%, which is excluded per your request).

### 5. Related context (qualitative, no additional dollar amounts)
- PwC's sole critical audit matter for fiscal 2024 was "Valuation of Inventories – Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments," citing the significant management judgment involved in future-demand and market-condition assumptions (p. 49).
- Risk factors (pp. 16–17) note that NVIDIA wrote down inventory, incurred cancellation penalties, and recorded impairments in the past, and that fiscal 2024 purchase commitments were affected by shortening lead times.

## JPMorgan Chase & Co. — 2023 Form 10-K (TDR accounting guidance adoption, January 1, 2023)

**Standard adopted:** FASB ASU 2022-02, *Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures* (eliminated TDR accounting/disclosure requirements, including the mandatory discounted cash flow (DCF) measurement of the allowance for TDRs). Adopted **January 1, 2023 under the modified retrospective method** (Note 1, p. 173 of the 10-K; Note 13, p. 256; MD&A "Accounting and Reporting Developments," p. 159).

### Amounts (millions of dollars)

| Item | Amount | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| Allowance for credit losses (Firm total) | **$(587)** — net **decrease** | Cumulative effect (balance-sheet, pre-tax) of adopting the new TDR guidance on the Firm's allowance for credit losses at January 1, 2023. Because the allowance for lending-related commitments was "NA" (no effect), this equals the total allowance for loan losses impact. |
| Allowance for loan losses — Consumer, excluding credit card | **$(489)** | Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle on the allowance for loan losses for the consumer (ex-card) portfolio segment. |
| Allowance for loan losses — Credit card | **$(100)** | Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle on the allowance for loan losses for the credit card portfolio segment. |
| Allowance for loan losses — Wholesale | **$2** | Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle on the allowance for loan losses for the wholesale portfolio segment (a small increase). |
| Retained earnings | **$446** increase, **after-tax** | Equity effect (net-of-tax) of the adoption, recorded as a "Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" in the Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity. Predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card. |

### Supporting points from the filing

- **Sources:** Note 1 (p. 173) and Note 13 (p. 256) state the guidance "was adopted on January 1, 2023 under the modified retrospective method which resulted in a net decrease to the allowance for credit losses of $587 million and an increase to retained earnings of $446 million, after-tax, predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card."
- **MD&A (p. 131 and Note 13, p. 260):** "The allowance for credit losses also reflected a reduction of $587 million as a result of the adoption of changes to the TDR accounting guidance on January 1, 2023."
- **Segment-level detail:** The $489 / $100 / $2 amounts are presented as the "Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle" row in the "Allowance for credit losses and related information" table (MD&A p. 132; Note 13 p. 258), which is disaggregated by **portfolio segment** (consumer excluding credit card, credit card, wholesale) — not by business segment (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM). No business-segment-level allowance effect is disclosed.
- **Reason for the reduction:** The Firm elected to move modified loans to troubled borrowers from an asset-specific (DCF) allowance to its non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance for all portfolios except collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual risk-rated loans (which remain asset-specific). The resulting lower expected credit losses reduced the allowance.
- **Reconciling equity figure:** The Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity (p. 169) show a 2023 "Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" of **$449 million** in retained earnings. That total combines the $446 million TDR adoption effect plus an immaterial (~$3 million) retained-earnings effect from the same-day adoption of the portfolio-layer fair value hedging method (HTM-to-AFS transfer), per Note 1.
- **Other context:** The adoption also eliminated the TDR "reasonably expected" and "concession" assessment criteria, so the Firm's 2023 modification population (FDMs) differs from prior-period TDRs — e.g., 2023 credit card FDMs of $648 million versus 2022 new TDRs of $418 million, and $27 million of trial modifications not treated as FDMs.

**1. Total expected separation cost: "approximately $700 million"**

- Verbatim: "We expect to incur **costs of approximately $700 million in connection with separating Upjohn**, of which, **approximately 75% has been incurred since inception and through December 31, 2021**. - What it represents: a forward-looking total of all costs Pfizer expects to incur in connection with the separation of the Upjohn Business, with roughly three-quarters already incurred as of the December 31, 2021 balance sheet date. It is stated as an approximate total (not a single line item).

**2. Separation-related costs incurred in 2020: "$434 million"**

The $700 million is the aggregate expected charge for the separation as a whole; the $434 million and $83 million are the amounts already incurred and recognized in discontinued operations in 2020 and 2019 respectively. ### The stated reason: COVID‑19's severe, early impact on commercial aviation and aerospace
The filing's core explanation is that the **initial effects of the COVID‑19 pandemic on commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers were "particularly severe."** Note 13 frames the reevaluation as arising from "the disruptions arising from the COVID‑19 pandemic, which we believed most significantly affected the **air travel, commercial aerospace and supporting industries**."

- **Employment levels and aircraft orders**
- **Announcements by manufacturers of reduced aircraft production**

Berkshire Hathaway's 2024 Form 10-K (BRK_2024_10K.pdf) gives the rationale in two places — the MD&A discussion of BHE and Note 26 on business segment data.

**1. It reflects how the energy businesses are actually managed and evaluated.**
In the MD&A (page K-43), Berkshire states directly: *"The discussion of BHE's operating results that follows is based on after-tax earnings, reflecting how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated."* BHE's results are therefore presented and discussed on an after-tax basis, with a segment table of "net earnings attributable to BHE" (U.S. utilities, natural gas pipelines, other energy businesses, real estate brokerage, and corporate interest and other) rather than the pre-tax earnings used for the manufacturing, service and retailing groups.

**2. Income taxes are considered at BHE specifically because of the magnitude of production tax credits and related regulatory effects.**
Note 26 (page K-109) contrasts BHE with the other non-insurance businesses: *"For most non-insurance businesses, pre-tax earnings are considered in allocating resources and capital, although income taxes are also considered at BHE, given the magnitude of production tax credits associated with wind-powered electricity generation investments and the related impacts from regulation."* In other words, the tax effects at BHE are not routine or incidental — they are large and unusual enough (driven by wind PTCs and the regulatory treatment of the related wind tax-equity investments) that the chief operating decision maker (the Chairman/CEO and the Vice Chairman of Non-Insurance Operations) evaluates BHE's results on an after-tax basis when allocating resources and capital.

**Why this matters in practice, as the numbers illustrate:**
- BHE's income taxes are a *benefit*, not a charge: pre-tax earnings of $2,292 million in 2024 became net earnings after income taxes of $4,163 million (effective income tax rate of **(81.6)%** in 2024, (215.1)% in 2023, (51.8)% in 2022), with the footnote noting the benefit "includes significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation." A pre-tax measure would therefore give a badly distorted view of BHE's economics.
- The utility rate-setting mechanism reinforces this: as the MD&A notes, "the rates BHE's regulated businesses charge customers for energy and services are largely based on the costs of business operations, including income taxes and a return on capital, and are subject to regulatory approval," so after-tax earnings are the measure that ties to the businesses' regulated economics.
- The tax/regulatory items flow through the after-tax discussion in the year-by-year analysis, e.g., 2024 U.S. utilities net earnings rose $1.1 billion (116.4%) partly on "income tax benefits from recognized wind production tax credits ($157 million)," and Northern Powergrid's 2024 improvement reflected "lower income tax expense attributable to charges recognized in 2023 for the U.K. Energy Profits Levy and a group relief tax benefit recognized in 2024."

## Boeing's delivery-linked causes for lower 2024 commercial airplane deliveries

**The facts:** BCA deliveries fell to **348 aircraft in 2024 from 528 in 2023**, with declines in every model (737: 265 vs. 396; 767: 18 vs. 32; 777: 14 vs. 26; 787: 51 vs. 73). (The one-unit 747 difference is simply the end of that program — final 747 delivery occurred in February 2023 — not a disruption cause.)

Boseing's 10-K links the decline to **five** causes it ties directly to deliveries:

**1. The 737-9 grounding and post-accident FAA action (Alaska Airlines, Jan. 5, 2024).** The FAA grounded the ~220 in-service 737-9 fleet and required enhanced inspections; all 737-9s in production had to complete that inspection before delivery. The FAA's quality-control investigation led to increased oversight, and the FAA "will not approve production rate increases beyond 38 per month or additional production lines until Boeing has complied with required quality and safety standards." Boeing's safety and quality plan slowed rates and delayed planned increases to reduce traveled work. The filing's cash-flow discussion confirms the linkage: "slowed and/or paused production **and lower deliveries** as a result of ongoing safety and quality improvement actions."

**2. The IAM 751 work stoppage (Sept. 13 – early Dec. 2024).** The filing states this in terms: "The IAM 751 work stoppage **significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024**." Production was paused on 737, 767, 777 and 777X (and BDS commercial derivatives KC-46A and P-8A), resuming in December.

**3. Supply chain constraints/disruptions and labor instability.** The filing says Boeing and its suppliers faced "supply chain disruptions as a result of production quality issues, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability," which "reduced overall productivity," and in the cash-flow discussion ties "supply chain constraints" directly to "lower deliveries." Concretely, 787 production was slowed below 5 per month on supply chain constraints and other production issues; the 767 line experienced "factory disruption, including supply chain delays and quality issues."

**4. Delays in certification/entry into service of new models and derivatives, plus the 777X ramp slowdown.** 737-7 and 737-10 certification was delayed (including the engine anti-ice engineering solution), leaving ~35 aircraft in inventory undeliverable. For the 777X, flight-test and certification delays pushed first 777-9 delivery to 2026, the 777-8 Freighter to 2028 and 777-8 passenger to not before 2030; Boeing "decided to slow the production rate ramp of 777X... which resulted in higher production costs **and further customer delivery delays**." The filing notes that "The production slow-down, the IAM 751 work stoppage and new agreement, and the timing of minor model certifications" together hurt 2024 performance, and that 737-7/-10 timing is set by the FAA.

**5. 787-specific delivery issues: business class seat delays and required rework.** "Delays associated with business class seats adversely impacted 2024 deliveries and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025." Separately, ~25 787s built prior to 2023 required inspection/rework, with most to be delivered in 2025 (the $256 million of related costs are abnormal production costs). The filing describes ~55 pre-2023-built 737-8s (including ~40 for China customers) as inventory to be delivered in 2025 — i.e., delivery timing pushed out of 2024.

## What I excluded (causes given only for production rates, costs or revenue)

- **777X/767 reach-forward losses of $4,079 million** and reduced BCA margins — earnings/cost items, not delivery causes.
- **$443 million of 737-9 customer considerations** and the associated concessions liability — a revenue/Sales-of-products charge, not a delivery driver.
- **IAM 751 new-contract pay increases, non-union pay enhancements, inflation, and $1,271 million of lower abnormal production costs** — cost/margin drivers.
- **The FAA's 38-per-month rate cap and planned rate increases** are only counted to the extent the filing itself links the resulting slowed/paused production to lower deliveries; where the filing discusses rates purely for cost or margin purposes (e.g., 767 "higher near-term production costs"), it is excluded.
- Forward-looking items (2025 certification timing, U.S.–China trade risk, FAA shutdown risk) and BDS program charges (KC-46A, T-7A, etc.) are not 2024 delivery causes.

**Bottom line: five delivery-linked causes — the 737-9 grounding and FAA-imposed production limits, the IAM 751 strike, supply chain/labor disruptions, certification and 777X ramp delays, and 787 seat/rework issues.**

**Inventory provisions and excess inventory purchase obligations.** This is the other quantified margin item the 10-K discusses (p. 42; also in Critical Accounting Estimates, p. 39):

**Cost-of-revenue composition and macro/supply-chain cost pressures.** The 10-K describes what flows through cost of revenue — primarily semiconductor costs (wafer fabrication, assembly, testing and packaging, board and device costs, manufacturing support costs and labor/overhead, final test yield fallout, memory and component costs, tariffs, and shipping), plus inventory and warranty provisions, acquisition-related intangible amortization, license/development and service arrangement costs, IP-related costs, and stock-based compensation for manufacturing personnel (p. 42).
